utterances.text: Well, I thought implicit in his question was the fact that he didn't take any pictures because he didn't want to take -- to waste film but we do have photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour. We're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- referring to the trips he said he took in the weeks after Operation Storm which is August 1995 which is his testimony that he saw 200 houses hit. The fact that he -- we've had this discussion already about when these other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear. Please, Mr. Misetic, perhaps put the question again to the witness perhaps in a briefer way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, you're taking trips in August, it is an obviously very important issue in the international community, you say you saw evidence of indiscriminate shelling --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- and your testimony is you have the one UN camera but didn't want to waste film?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, I did take photographs, Your Honour. And I sent those photographs to our office in Zagreb headquarters, some of them. I was informed that UNMOs would make a detailed survey of the houses and that also a team from mission headquarters would come and make a further detailed assessment of buildings, because it was a very controversial issue and my feeling was there was a feeling from mission headquarters of maybe objectivity or assessment of what is really damage, collateral damage, severe damage, as is analysed here. If I'm not mistaken, and correct me if I'm wrong, does this document and this report continue with anything more than this? Is it going on to many pages? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There is one page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, we're not at this moment discussing this, Mr. Roberts. The question was put to you mainly seeking confirmation why you did not photograph. You said you made some pictures. Are those among the pictures we've seen? Are they in any of the series? And we're talking about damage in the city of Knin caused by the taking over 4th of August, 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had taken a number of photographs only two of which had been passed to the investigation, and I sent, and it wasn't many, maybe a roll of film, up to our mission headquarters in Zagreb, with other photographs on, of the shelling of buildings and general decay in Banja Luka towards about the third week of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer correctly, you said I made some photographs, although we have not seen them, so we don't know what they're focussing on, and apart from that it was not my primary task and I understood that reporting would be done by others and most likely by other means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You've stated that you've seen the UNMO report, you saw it back then, yet you've given a conclusion that the shelling was indiscriminate and that 200 civilian buildings were hit. What specific evidence did you hear of or do you have that contradicts the conclusions in the UNMO report on your screen?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to subscribe and I haven't got them with me the reports I read at the time and over the two or three weeks from UNMOs from the sector commander's office and from offices of civil affairs who had lived in Knin during the time of the shelling, and that information was discussed at the time and conclusions were drawn and that information was sent to headquarters Zagreb on a daily basis. I haven't access to it but I felt that was a general overall impression of a good many people from headquarters Sector South from different UN departments, especially, if I could add, people who were in Knin, international civilians and others on, the morning of the 4th of August when the bombardment started and were picked up over two or three hours following by an APC or more than APC in the same way as I was picked up from my accommodation. So, again, I'm very, very surprised then and now at this report, which, I expressed at the time, well, forgive me, it's three paragraphs. Do we have something more, please, than this, at this stage, 18th of August, and there was quite a defensive response by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit P228, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is an UN CIVPOL assessment performed on 18 August by officers, Thor Hansen, Steinar Hagvag, Steinar Hagvag, and they were surveying Knin to determine the damage caused by shelling, arson and wilful damage. If we could scroll down a little bit, please? We covered the whole township and observed several impacts of shells, rockets around the Tvik factory, milicija headquarters, general direction of the northern barracks and between the government house, Knin radio TV building and hillside below Knin castle. We counted roughly 20 houses buildings hit by shells and about another 20 presumable damaged by arson. And it goes on to talk about on the main street most noticeable are totally gutted by fire. On the positive side we found the area south of Knin hospital unharmed. Even the satellite antenna and the ECMM accommodation looked 100 per cent intact. The best part of the damage is obviously not caused by direct acts of war, exchange of fire but wilful damage inflicted by liberation forces. Now this is UN CIVPOL's assessment on the same day, 18th of August. Did you receive a copy of this report?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this report also does not suggest that -- this report also does not suggest that there was indiscriminate shelling of civilian targets on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document does not say that or suggest that, no. And I had a discussion with the Steinar about the time of this document, after seeing it and reading it, as I understand, and the Court will know better, but I understand there are other documents also on this issue conducted later and even before this document. I do not think for the Court record that these two documents seen from UNMOs and CIVPOL are the only reports made by UN officials in regard to the shelling of Knin on the 4th and 5 of August. I think there are other documents that suggest a different picture that are available to this Chamber. Whether they will be submitted, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, please identify by name the persons that we can contact who would have drafted those reports which contradict these two reports.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall now by name, but I can attempt to find them out from personal records of UN employees that worked in Sector South at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, let me turn to your personal observations on the morning of the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Before I turn to that, Mr. Roberts, are you aware that -- based on your conversations with the Office of the Prosecutor in recent weeks are aware that the senior UNMO, the Senior Military Observer, Steinar Hjertnes, has told the Office of the Prosecutor that he filed a final assessment of the shelling and that it was consistent with the findings in the provisional assessment? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware he has appeared before the Court I'm aware that a final assessment was sent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How are you aware that a final assessment was sent, by UNMO?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at the time I knew a final assessment report was being sent to Zagreb headquarters. I think we had several conversations in the UNMO office about a further assessment to the one I was shown now, in terms of the 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in those conversations with UNMO at the time, they told you that the further assessment was consistent with the initial assessment. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I recall seeing the final document that went up and that it concurred with their initial assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just add one point in terms of this final issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is suggesting from the report I'm seeing on the screen that my information in my statements is incorrect. I can only refer Chamber and the Court to witnesses who were in Knin on the morning of the 4th and 5th, and I know that they submitted reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, whether these documents suggest that your assessment is wrong or whether your assessment suggests that the reports are wrong is something the Chamber will have to consider at a later stage, and advice to the Court as to whom should be called as witnesses, first of all, in this procedural system it's mainly left to the parties, although the Court has an opportunity to call witnesses if it wishes to do so, but I think advice at this point either to the parties or to the Court is, however good your intentions may be, is not the real thing we're waiting for. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, turning to P676, which is your 1998 witness statement, at page 3 towards the top, second -- third -- second full paragraph towards the middle, it says: "Shortly before 0500 hours at about 0450 hours I was surprised to see an UN mini-bus drive rapidly along the side street in the direction of my apartment building. It was accompanied by an UN jeep." And if we could go to P677, page 4, on the bottom paragraph you say: "On the morning of the 4th of August, 1995, I was asleep in my apartment on the top third floor of a block of apartments in Knin when I was awakened by a sudden crash of heavy explosives just before 5.00 a.m." My question to you is were you awake at 4.50 observing UN vehicles or were you asleep and awoken at around 5.00 a.m. by artillery?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general paragraph here is not correct. This statement was made in 2007 to an investigator. That is completely true the date of the statement is made. And the better recollection for sure which this whole episode of the shelling something described is in the 1998 statement and I prefer that that's the one that I think is much more realistic, in terms of what I remember and recall at that time from 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is there a reason that you didn't correct that as you reviewed it to testify before the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the general reflection of what happened but not in detail, and I did not correct it, no. But that is the reason why I'm pointing out, albeit late now, that 1991 is the one that's much closer to the time of the events concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now in your 1998 statement at page 4, you say at the top of the page: "The last Radio Knin broadcast was I think about 0500 hours warning the public of the incoming attack." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you bring that up on the -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sure. That is P676.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Must be a mistake on the record where you refer to 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd read the portion, the sentence previously begins: "The radio and TV studio building behind the main street in the centre of town was apparently hit in the early morning barrage." Then it says: "The last Radio Knin broadcast was, I think about 0500 hours warning the public of the incoming attack." Now, did you hear the broadcast?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear the broadcast directly. We took a quick summary from a taped version of the broadcast that was going on but there were also, not here, I was aware later that there were other broadcasts of Radio Knin during the day but the focus of warning the public of the incoming attack was of what was going on on that morning. And I think there were actually three broadcasts of Radio Knin during the course of the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is there any particular reason you have said in the statement in 1998 that the last radio broadcast was at 0500 hours and connecting it in context of saying the radio and TV studio building behind the main street in the centre of town was apparently hit in the early morning barrage of 4 August 1995? Is it fair to say that in 1998 you were saying that the early barrage hit Radio Knin and that that resulted in Radio Knin going off the air?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I recall there was a broadcast early morning about the shelling and what was happening and in general a very blurred picture of a radio news broadcast. I don't think that that was going -- in terms of the building being hit and then going off the air, that this was the last broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How did Radio Knin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, on the French transcript, the beginning of your question was not yet translated, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How did Radio Knin know that an attack was coming?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have put here the last radio broadcast, I think, about 0500 hours warning the public, but the nature of the broadcast was about the attack as well as what was happening by revealing the bombardment that was not just in Knin but through the general area of the so-called Krajina that an attack was taking place in many cities. And the later broadcasts of that echo that. It is not accurate here the way it is interpreted I can see the way isn't it warning the public as if it's an announcement there's going to be an attack. I'm sorry about that, but that's not the way in which the broadcast was heard. It was about the bombardment being in many areas throughout the so-called Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now in your statements and I won't go through them all, but if you don't mind I will read them to you and if you need to see them, we'll show them to you. In 1998 you said at page 2: "We had not managed to even dress properly and hit the floor together in the central lobby of their second floor apartment below my own." In P677, which is 28 February 2007: "I leapt out of bed and immediately became aware that incoming artillery shells were coming from the Croatian positions on the Dinara mountain above Knin. I headed for safety down to the second floor landing where I was joined by Nevis, her sister and her sister's husband and their young son." Now, sir, is it fair to say that for a large portion of the shelling, you were -- and you had sought shelter on the second floor for your own personal safety?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And again if I'm not mistaken, I describe that in my 1998 statement in those paragraphs that run consecutively as I recall. We were there on the second floor central part of the building from the moments when the shelling began for at least 45 minutes, maybe an hour. I think I have said this more previously in the statement. Hearing the bombardment going overhead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to P677, please. Page 4, please. At the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in that bottom paragraph you describe what you saw from the balcony and you say, the last sentence: "After about an hour I went back to my apartment and I could see smoke rising from the," if we can go to the next page, please, at the top, "direction of the RSK government building as well as a fuel depot located quite close to the RSK government building. However, I was also aware of smoke rising from the top of civilian apartments in various parts of town," and then it goes on.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, is until your statement of July 1, 2008, which is a little more than three weeks ago, in none of your statements, and you gave five of them, did you ever say anything about seeing dead bodies from your balcony. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on the 4th of August, one of your primary responsibilities was to communicate what was happening in Knin with the domestic and international press. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once I got to headquarters, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could call up, please -- sorry, Your Honour. 1D41-0311. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a Reuters report from 4 August 1995 talking about what is happening. It says towards the middle of that page, it's a paragraph starting: "UN spokesman in Knin, Alun Roberts, said peacekeepers saw civilian who had been wounded in the bombardment but said it was difficult to gauge how many people were injured."

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a question or can I comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to take you through, if necessary, several of these reports, none of which have you saying, We know of at least two casualties because I saw them myself. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can certainly. I have said it in my statement before. My view personally on the ground as a spokesperson was to be very cautious and not to go out with anything because I had to be in touch with my press office in Zagreb. I was not sure there would be a standard press line coming from out from Zagreb. I was aware that was an attack that was not just on Knin. Other parts of the sector were being affected as well as Sector North and therefore I was, as I said in my statement, very cautious, I wanted to be cautious before I went out and started saying, Well, I have a particular person who saw three people, that's very, very tempting to do but not in the first hours of 4th August 1995 and that is not the first time that I found myself in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, I could take you through these various Reuters reports. I won't. Suffice it to say that they all quote you and none of them quote you as identifying any persons having been killed that you had seen. I note your answer. My question to you then is: If you didn't mention it on the 4th, what precluded you in five witness statements to the Office of the Prosecutor from bringing it up then?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had recalled in 2007 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. The sequence of my statements with the first one in 1997, which did not deal with the bombardment, and then I was asked by the Tribunal investigators to prepare another statement, which would be focussed very much on the issue of the bombardment, which I did in 1998 and submitted it. There was then a ten-year gap between any further contact by investigators from ICTY to visit myself to follow up. I had thought in the intervening period that that 1998 statement covered all dimensions of the attack and what I had seen, including what I had seen from my balcony. In making the last statement, I was asked, Okay, and did you see personally any bodies or people hit or killed, and then I put in yes, I recall from the balcony I saw two and I thought a third. And that went in very late. But I had thought that some of that was in the 1998 statement and it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit D711, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D711 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I may have 1D41-0293.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, what I'm going to show you is a Croatian document noting a conversation that you had on the 4th of August. The document itself is from the 4th of August, between you as the UN spokesmen in Sector South and the conversation you had with Mr. Stojan Obradovic who worked for the Stina news agency. Do you recall him?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall the news agency in Split, Stina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to just take this through the time of the interview purports to at 1415 hours on 4 August 1995. At the bottom of the second paragraph, speaking of you it said: "He said that the repeated shelling of the town centre, Knin, had occurred approximately 25 minutes ago" --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just which paragraph are we on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, last sentence. "And that the situation at the moment was calm." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is it also subject of statements made by UN spokesperson 4th August at around 14, 1500 concerning events in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So he is dating that in the early afternoon of the 4th of August, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the fourth paragraph : "Asked by Obradovic on the situation in the town regarding the civilians, Roberts said there was no panic among the civilians. However, in his opinion the people were extremely shocked and surprised by the shelling this morning. Apartments have been destroyed and many window and shops -- shop windows broken. "When asked whether there were any fatally wounded he answered that they had contacted with the Knin hospital at which they were told that there was a need for assistance and supplies. "Furthermore, Roberts said that they were willing to provide assistance as much as they could..." and then it goes on, last sentence there: "No information was available on the number of seriously wounded persons." If we could turn to the next page, please. The second-to-last sentence which begins in the middle: "Asked by Obradovic on how the people would react if the Croatian army entered Knin, he answered that he did not want to be speculative about that. However, that the people in Knin were in an extremely serious situation, very much concerned and anxious during the shelling but still not asking for their assistance in order to leave or abandon the said area. He noted that the situation in Knin was extremely serious."

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, a few questions on that. First, you will note again that in this interview, when asked specifically about fatally wounded, you did not respond by saying that you had personally witnessed two fatally wounded persons. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And I had been in touch with my -- with my press office colleagues in Zagreb and I understood that an assessment was being done of a broader nature by the various civilian elements that had come into headquarters in the morning as well as people in Sector South command headquarters to put out something towards Zagreb mid-afternoon for an update. So I didn't want to go after the conversation with Christopher Gunness and make any kind of personal observations when I felt a larger picture was being presented at the mission headquarters press office. And this paragraph here, I think -- I think sums it up pretty well of being very much inside the box, when quite a few other people were running around wanting to say and I think did say various information that was not consistent. These are people that I think responded to the press before I got to the Sector South headquarters that I learned about later about what they had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, following up on that second response, you said this was -- it sums up pretty well being very much inside the box.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It also sums up well, does it not, that at the moment that you were speaking with this reporter at 1415, there was no panic among the civilians. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 1415 we had, yes, I think there was no visible sign of panic. I had been in the town about an hour before this phone call from Stina and we had, as you saw on the videotape, the ad hoc press briefing by General Forand accompanied by myself in the centre of town in the ex-former so-called RSK government headquarters restaurant and we had seen coming away from there, ten minutes, people beginning to put things in cars, there was debris on the streets and there was the first signs of people preparing to leave to go. There was no kind of visible sense of people panic. People were asking us what was going on, but that's all. But I didn't sort of see, I said here, a visible sign of emotion, panic at that time which would about an hour or half-hour before this comment to Stina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit D712, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D712 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Misetic, I notice that we had ten minutes delay in our start, even a bit more, you said you would finish by the second break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have, and I was going to ask for the Trial Chamber's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have one topic. I will tell you it is to cover the issue of the evacuation. The witness was I believe personally present at some discussions. I would finish it in lest than 15 minutes, Your Honour, unless Mr. Waespi needs some extra time in which case I would cut it shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I need about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About 15 minutes. Now, of course, it is it usually preferable to have the break just prior to the start of the re-examination, but I'm looking at our interpreters and transcribers, whether they would insist on having a break now, no, not insisting on. This is the communication, the unspoken with our interpreters. Mr. Misetic, I'll strictly keep you to not one second more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just note that I'm sure the interpreters wish there was more unspoken communication by me today, but I thank them for their indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, let me take you to this issue of evacuation. In your 2007 statement, you talked about arriving back -- let me find it. When you arrived back in Sector South after your vacation, which I believe you said was on the 3rd of August when you arrived. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You said that you had heard in 2007 and let me quote it: "When I first arrived back in Knin after my vacation, I had learned from the office of the Sector South commander of what had been a rather unusual follow-up to a meeting earlier in July 1995 for UN assistance for the evacuation of the civilian population of Knin in the event of an attack by the Croatian army?" Do you recall making that statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do and subsequently it is very important to add right here that there was discussion with investigates concerning the document that described that discussion and it was clearly assessed that that type of document could not have been made on the date concerned, but I had recalled general discussion of something being told me about assistance request if things got out of hand, developments. I recalled long time ago in 2007 to 1995, but at the time I came back something like that was in my mind and then I related that to this page that has this odd date of July 1995 on. But as has been clarified in going through that document specifically, in what that says, that date is clearly wrong and the real significant assistance of UN request was discussions on the 4th of August. But I can recall that on coming back being told something by two officials in the commander's office of something earlier being discussed generally should things be getting to a very difficult stage but not in terms of assistance from the UN in characterizing what that really was. And we spent a fair bit of time going through this with the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, just as a technical matter, when I pause after your answer, it is because I'm trying to let the interpreters catch up, so if you then continue to fill the pause, we never catch up, just so we can assist the interpreters. Thank you. Now, let's talk about what you just said, that on the 4th of August there were more -- the really significant UN assistance was on the 4th of August. Can you explain in more detail what discussions took place between the UN and the RSK about providing evacuation assistance?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for me, the -- the issue, as I recall, was raised by a journalist at the about 12.00 noon press briefing in Knin, and I think it was Worldwide Television news, a local crew, that asked a question and I'm now paraphrasing what may have been introduced into evidence by General Forand, so I don't want to go and restate that, but as I recall he responded that -- it was a question more or less like what are the UN doing to assist and provide support to help people leave or provide petrol, and the general reply, well, forgive me, we are the UN and your authorities are responsible for those things and that there had been no real contact from the RSK political and military in regard to requesting assistance in any clear-cut manner. It was later in the afternoon that we began to see things change and as I said in my statement people arriving outside the gates of Sector South headquarters and then the picture changed quite quickly in a few hours, and then there was a meeting in the evening that was supposed to take place between the so-called RSK authorities and Sector South headquarters but as far as I know, there was no actual presence of UN personnel that went to that meeting. It didn't take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know if General Forand went to have a meeting with the ARSK representatives at about 1800 in the evening of the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood him to go downtown for that meeting, yes. And I refer to that -- I'm not sure and he will have told you if he has been before the Court what happened. But I'm not sure that people from the with RSK in any real responsible positions were present to have that dialogue and discussion. I know that the general came back really, in my view, quite frustrated about what these people were trying to do, look what's going on and what they're asking was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going to say way beyond what the UN could really lend itself to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was Kostan Ovakovic [phoen] a responsible RSK official?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't want you do that.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Okay. But I've met him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have -- Mr. Roberts, I'm sorry, I have five minutes, so I don't want to you speculate.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'll be very direct, then. My view of Mr. Ovakovic was not being very organised and being rather idealistic and descriptive and not really realistic in the weeks preceding as to what really was happening around Knin militarily or other developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in your 2007 statement at page 6 that you were present at the press conference - we saw the video earlier - he said he was having trouble making contact with RSK authorities but that he mentioned that sometime before, there had been a request from RSK authorities for UN assistance to evacuate a large number of civilians. However, as no plan or follow-up had been received -- just, sorry for the translators. Is that referring to the July conversations that you've testified about already?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not. I think it is referring very much to that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So earlier in the day there had been some request from RSK authorities to provide UN assistance to evacuate civilians?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there had been a meeting before the press briefing, but I'm not sure. General Forand perhaps would refer to that. But even then, I think it was along the lines of the UN at the Sector South commander's level wanting to know precisely what it was that they needed and it was not being presented in a written form. A later meeting was supposed to happen quickly or soon after to devise that, and this is what was referred to as the 1800 meeting and I recall the general coming back and nothing had been concluded. It was really almost too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D41-0341, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I add, Your Honour, on just the very same issue or time is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Briefly. I'll look at the clock and I will not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Give credit to you, Mr. Misetic. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also in the aspect of time, all I remember is that we found ourselves mid-evening negotiating with the several hundred Serb civilians with tractors, trailers, whatever, outside the gates about what we could do to assist them and making them have two clear choices, which I described in my statement what they were, to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 30 seconds credit, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, you will note that this is a report of a broadcast on Serbian Radio Belgrade on 4 August 1995. It's at 2200 CET, which is 20 GMT. Is it General Mrksic on giving an interview and if I can find the right portion. Towards the middle there, he says: "No, the disengagement line has not been changed. Our forces have withdrawn to positions for the direct defence of Knin." And above that -- sorry. That is what I was looking for: "The aggression that started at 0500 continued until night-fall. Combat operations in the Knin region have been suspended for the moment. Knin is in darkness and the population is being evacuated." In your statement you said that you were monitoring Radio Knin and didn't hear anything about an evacuation order having been issued. Is it possible, sir, that General Mrksic was on Radio Belgrade, made the announcement that there had been an evacuation order but that it wasn't on the Radio Knin because it had been knocked out for the shelling. And if you could pause for the interpreters, please?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen this document before, in terms of Mr. Mrksic's statement from Belgrade, I believe, and I was really surprised when I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I tender this --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I felt it was covered up after the event by people who had left or were in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is from the 4th of August, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm saying that, that this person is speaking, as I understand, from?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. He is on Radio Belgrade from Knin.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I tender the document, Your Honour, and I have one more document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit D713, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D713 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Last topic, sir, 1D41-0343.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a New York Times article. I'm sure you saw it last night, December 12, 1995, talking about everything that had happened after Operation Storm. If we could go to the next page. At the bottom, please. You are quoted as follows: "There has not been an organised government campaign to harass, loot, and kill people,' said Alun Roberts, a United Nations spokesman, 'but there has been no sincere organised attempt by the authorities to control the situation." Does that statement that you made to the New York Times accurately reflect your view of what took place?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question put by the journalist was broader and this is an portion of my answer, but that's what I, said, that there has been no -- not been an organised government campaign. I would just ask the Chamber, please, to also reflect on my other statements and those especially made by my spokesperson colleagues from Zagreb mission headquarters, in the context of this. To pull out one is not really saying that is the whole sweep of the UN's scope of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit D714, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Roberts, for testifying, and I thank the Trial Chamber for the extra time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break and we'll resume at five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have three short, I hope, topics to cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The first one, Mr. Roberts, is following up on a question by Mr. Misetic before the break. The so-called final assessment of the SMO and that refers to Prosecution Exhibit 64, the two-page document. Do you recall, Mr. Roberts, has been shown to you. Now, you answered on an inquiry whether you had heard of any -- any final assessment, you said, yes, you recall seeing a final assessment, a follow-up to P64, and you also said that it was consistent with the initial assessment. Now where did you see that document?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, in the office of the UN Military Observers in Sector South headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was there a person who directed you to or how did you come across the document?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just regular daily visits and discussions with UNMOs in the UNMO office downstairs on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how big was the document, how many pages, if more than one page?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was more than one page. I thought it was quite a substantial document, going through various parts of Knin. It was an assessment report. I didn't go and read it there and then or anything, but I was shown it as what's being sent in to the mission headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you have a copy, did you make a copy of the document?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I did. I'm not completely sure. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall the date?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be some -- I'm only speculating now, not being sure. Sometime middle September, I think, something like that. It was certainly a few weeks after the 18th of August initial provisional assessment that was shown me just now. That was the date, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you discuss it with its author, the SMO?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have a conversation with Steinar about this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts. Let's turn to a second brief issue, the -- your UN interpreter. Who picked Mr. Predrag Sare as your UN interpreter?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was assigned and recruited for employment before I arrived in September 1993. He would have gone through the normal process of employing interpretation staff by having to go fill in an application, be interviewed by personnel office, a background check would have had to have been done, and the panel who would interview him would be two or three people, usually somebody from personnel, somebody from the section who would employ him, which would be civil affairs overall, and one other person, usually a panel of three.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you involved in hiring him?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not in Sector South at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The other issue in connection to him, did you receive any complaints for instance witnesses who were interviewed a second time with a different interpreter that, you know, the first interview with Mr. Sare was not accurate? Have you ever heard of any such complaints?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To the contrary. I know when senior officials from headquarters in Zagreb, mission headquarters would come, quite often he would be assigned as the official interpreter at higher level meetings, the reason being purely on the need for very accurate fast interpretation not only in English but sometimes in different languages. French, I think, Swedish, Italian. He had a broad range of languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts. Let's turn to the last issue and that's something Mr. Kuzmanovic raised with you. He asked you whether you gave the licence plates, the sketch or the list with those licence plate numbers to the Croatian authorities, and you answered no. Now let me show you 65 ter 5323, which is one of the documents on the list to be tendered with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could go to page 5 at paragraph 18, and this is page 7 on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember having written a report on the Varivode incident, Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one second. Yes, I did write a report of the public information office on the whole of Varivode, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps -- I'm sorry, I should have done that, if we could see the first page first. Is that your report, Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the report, 3rd of October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Going back to page 5 at paragraph 18 and it is the last paragraph before paragraph 19, last subparagraph. It's on page 5 -- not on paragraph 5, page 5. Yes. Can you scroll down a little bit more, please. Yes, that's it. Let me read you what you wrote in October following the Varivode incident. "I subsequently learned tonight from UN CIVPOL's deputy sector chief, Lief Bjorken, present at the meeting today that they have asked the Croatian police in Zadar for copies of all documentation and full access to the investigation. (That would be a first time if it happens!)" Now, do you know whether it happened for the first time that UN CIVPOL got full access to an investigation site?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, if it did happen, it would be a first time, because of the actual request I knew had been made at several police stations for investigation reports. This was a serious incident and that's my rather sarcastic response back to myself, and later it is contrasted at the very end of that report in talking to Lief again that they had not got all documentation many weeks after the incident itself from the Zadar police. They couldn't talk anymore to the UN CIVPOL. It had been handed to the actual courts for processing, and the whole report concludes as is available to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What relevance does this have to whether or not plates were handed by Mr. Roberts -- it was obvious he didn't hand the plates in regarding the incident I crossed him on. What does this have to do with that? They're completely different issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next question, I believe, will reveal Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will wait for the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, returning to the issue of not providing these licence plate numbers to the Croatian police, based on your experience you gained in dealings with the Croatian authorities and their responses to your requests, do you think you would have gotten any response back from the Croatian authorities if you had given them the licence plate numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, that's complete explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, this really calls for speculation. You can ask the witness about when he made requests and, then of course we would have to consider requests which are of a similar kind as the matter we're dealing, which, by the way, is not a request but not providing information spontaneously, which is of course, so therefore the question is not only calling for speculation if any request -- if he would have done so, whether he would have had a response. I think the issue is whether, with due diligence, information was given to the police forces that would have to investigate so as to assist them, not necessarily to reach responses, that's what I understand to be the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if I might add, this is completely the reserve the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think I already pointed that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, ask whatever kind of factual questions but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- not the question you had just put to him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, can you let us know the reasons if there are any specific reasons why you did not pass on the list of licence plates to the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was, first, I had given this list to UN CIVPOL; I hope that is clear from what I said earlier. I understood they were in touch with the Croatian police in Knin and that was my feeling of chain of command. I don't want to say anything further but that is the way I passed it on in terms of CIVPOL having it, CIVPOL in touch with the police and whatever was going to happen would be used in that fashion or chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to 65 ter 5334. And Mr. President, that's the Robert Fisk article, the second one that has not been admitted based on your earlier ruling, but I believe that this issue opens the door to ask the witness for a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe its correct number is P687 MNA, marked non-admitted, I think is the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I'm interested in the second page, the last paragraph, and we already heard a couple of days ago who Mr. Fisk was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now I read you the last paragraph. And I quote: "The Croat interior ministry police, who are deeply implicated in the murders and burnings in Krajina claim they will investigate acts of arson or looting. Doubtless, they will be able to trace the two cars of the anonymous three Croat ethnic cleansers. The first, an Audi, carried the registration number ZD 570 H from the coastal town of Zadar, while the other bore the number plate KR 770 H, registered in Karlovac, 30 miles from Zagreb. Equally doubtless, however, the Croat police will not lift a finger to find out who owns the car, since they must know all too well."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no idea what the connection is with these license plates and this article with the incident that we're discussing in cross-examination and direct examination earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the questions to follow will shed some light on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, is the experience Mr. Fisk talks about in dealing with the Croatian police in relation to finding out about the owners of cars of suspected perpetrators consistent with your experience?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt Mr. Waespi, but first of all, Mr. Fisk who writes this article doesn't say that he dealt with the Croatian police. It has absolutely nothing to do with dealing with the Croatian police. He doesn't say who he talked to, he doesn't say what he dealt with, he doesn't say that he gave him the licence plate numbers. He doesn't say anything. It is an article expressing an opinion with a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first, Mr. Waespi, if you want to find out whether the experience of Mr. Fisk, whatever that exactly was, is consistent with the witness's own experience, first ask him about his own experience and then at least we have a starting point which is solid, and then the comparison to be made will depend on what the answer of the witness will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, were you involved in providing the Croatian police with information about alleged crimes you have witnessed in the Krajina following Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present with UN CIVPOL on several occasions when they gave information to the police authorities in Knin and subsequently to advise the Court, if I could, the -- there are more than maybe a dozen or more CIVPOL Knin reports of UN CIVPOL about incidents where they saw and recorded licence plate numbers of incidents of arson, looting and other violent acts and they gave those, that information of those incidents with what they saw of licence plates to the Knin authorities and that information should be, have been, tabled to the court authorities but exists certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And following up on your answer, did you every get the feedback by the Croatian police on what they did with this information? Did they report back and say, Yes, we received information, we followed up, that's what we are doing or what we did with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What information are we talking about? Are we talking in general, are we talking a specific incident? It's very broad and vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's split up the question in two portions. First, about what -- first, whether there was in the feedback on investigative steps on the event described in general terms; and then, second part, whether you ever received any feedback in relation to specifically licence plate numbers being investigated and results of such investigations. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Well, chain of command again it would not be that the police of Knin would report obviously to me, the press officer, but they report to CIVPOL and on many contacts with CIVPOL in Knin station and headquarters, my impression was from their reports to mission headquarters that there was no feedback of follow-up investigations when they had submitted oral and written information to the police, including on occasions information useful like licence plate numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I believe the witness answered the second question as well with his last point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think he did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, especially in light of the tendering of certainly a dozen of different newspaper articles over the last two days, Slobodna Dalmacija, New York Times today, I suggest also, given the witness's answer, that this exhibit should be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, I see a distinction between tendering a New York Times article which quotes the witness on the stand and putting the quote to the witness and taking an article which doesn't have any direct relationship to the witness and start putting newspaper articles in. I just wanted to note that distinction. With respect to the particular substance, I'll leave it to other counsel since the issue doesn't deal with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic rose before I did. I would join in that objection and especially considering the lack of relevance specifically to the issues that were covered in cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Slobodna Dalmacija was the exhibit that I put in, already in evidence before the Court because it directly referred to the accused and therefore, quoting him in the national press, it was a matter that was admissible and relevant but the Fisk article as we have seen causes all sort of evidential problems, and if the Court opens the door with this particular article one can foresee that many more can come through the door, because there is no basis between this witness's evidence and Mr. Fisk's experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, if there would be good reasons to admit this in evidence, then it would not be a problem to open the door because then there would be good reasons for similar evidence in the future, so that argument, as such, that it would have some follow-up, whether that is acceptable or not acceptable depends on the acceptability of the decision on this one. Let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I believe one of the issues brought by the Defence the last time we discussed this exhibit was that the author cannot be cross-examined. That applies to us as well. We cannot cross-examine or we could not, the author of not only Slobodna Dalmacija, also Vecernje List, and there are three -- D36, D37, D59, D38. I don't think all of them relate to direct quotes from the accused. It's about reliability, about giving weight, but I think also given the earlier link between Mr. Fisk and Mr. Roberts here who met each other before Mr. Fisk went out and what he said today clearly is enough of a foundation between this witness, the tendering witness and the evidence and that's all that matters in my view, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One observation, I'm sorry, every article produced by us mentions Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, there is no need for your observation because the Chamber does not reconsider its decision on the admission of the -- this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The last document I would like to show is a document which was on the list of exhibits, potential exhibits for Mr. Roberts from the Gotovina Defence and I'd like to call it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We earlier said that we do not reconsider. Of course the right language might have been that we have considered whether we should change our decision and that is of course a kind of reconsideration and that our conclusion is that we'll not give a decision different from the earlier. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This is 1D41-0114, a four-page document dated 19th October 1995, authored by the Republic of Croatia Ministry of the Interior, bureau for the protection of the constitutional order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it talks about various issues of Croatian intelligence into what the UNMOs were doing. And it has one reference to Mr. Roberts, and that's on page 3 of the English version. The third full paragraph, the large one starts: "The person drawing most attention both prior to and after Operation Storm is Alun Roberts from Wales who has been almost openly supporting the Serb side ever since he arrived in Knin up to the present days. He is highly appreciated among his colleagues for his professionalism and engagement in his mandate." And it goes on of course to discuss the connection between Mr. Roberts and Predrag Sare in whom it says here Mr. Roberts has great confidence. Is that an accurate reflection of the way you were perceived by your colleagues and the dealings with Mr. Sare as found out by the Croatian intelligence, Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their perception, and I can only speculate, I don't know whether it's accurate, but it came across to me that I was considered to be a sympathizer of the people in Knin with a particular allegiance to certain local people and to certain interpreters, and this was, just quickly, referred to and raised by the press colleagues in Zadar at the press briefing in open questions and given a quite clear descriptive response which was not reported by me in terms of way the UN works and how we go about being public information officers and how we are checked and how we conduct our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Croatian authorities, after Operation Storm, the end of Operation Storm, equally checked and looked into what the members of the UN were doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- before we deal with this question. The previous question, I thought that you were asking about how colleagues of Mr. Roberts appreciated him; that is, positive and professionalism and engagement in his mandate. And I got the impression from the answer that Mr. Roberts was not talking about that. So I first have to verify whether that was what you asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then I have to ask Mr. Roberts whether his answer was about how he was appreciated by his colleagues in terms of professionalism and commitment or that you were talking about how the Croatians or the Serbs, whomever may have appreciated you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is, first of all, that's how I perceive the view of the Croatian authorities would be towards me. In regard to colleagues, meaning UN colleagues, the answer would be, yes, I think that that's the viewpoint throughout. For information, usually public information officer of the UN or political affairs officers usually only stay one year in a mission area before they are transferred for a range of reasons, especially in conflict, but I continued there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi, it comes as a bit of a surprise that you ask about A, get an answer about B, and that you just go on to your next question. That suggests that you -- your question or the answer is not that much --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Maybe I wasn't following it as closely as I should have. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, and then the next question, let me first read it on my screen so that I know what the objection might be about. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can rephrase it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you rephrase it then we will see whether Mr. Misetic still has an objection. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, were you aware that the Croatian authorities were collecting information about your performance as a UN spokesperson post-Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had been drawn to my attention by UN security, as well as other UN officials had had contacts with the Croatian officials were also cautioned by those who would assist those things, like UN security, that this was more than likely and to take that into account. I'm seeing here, if I may, this reference in the centre, for what it's worth, if that is good official information, this is not true at all, and we have responded to this in those days gone by during the mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was going to bar table it so we have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we strike it from the list of the bar table documents and have a number assigned to it. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P694.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P694 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That concludes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, there was a question and answer series on the issue of UN CIVPOL and what was given to whom and when in various circumstances. I'm only concerned in this particular circumstance and that is the incident at Grubori. You did not give the licence plates to the Croatian police. That's already been established. You said that someone at UN CIVPOL told you that they, UN CIVPOL were in touch with the Croatian police. Who at UN CIVPOL was in touch with the Croatian police regarding these licence plates, when, and what was that person's name at Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the names of the person at the Croatian police specifically. I understood from UN CIVPOL operations officer on that night that the on-duty operations officer was the person informed as well as the station commander of the station in Knin from the actual UN CIVPOL UN commander in Sector South headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Those are titles. I want names, sir.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't have them. I don't recall them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you can't tell me when and with whom at the Croatian police anyone spoke to about providing these license plates that you wrote down. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information that that was passed on in terms of a photocopy or directly, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you met with either a representative of General Cermak or other people relating to this incident and you did not provide any of those people with those licence plate numbers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we met with Mr. Dondo, no, I did not give a document of that kind. It was only in the afternoon I recorded the actual license plate numbers the second time we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. There is a question about your perceived --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The last series of questions in which you were shown the document about the issue of professionalism and/or bias, you currently live in the capital of Republic of Srpska, Banja Luka, which is not exactly a symbol of diversity and ethnic tolerance, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I wouldn't agree with you at all. I have lived in Banja Luka but also have a range of other locations and friends throughout the whole of the Balkans that I resided and stay with, so your reflection there of that reflecting something on somebody's character, I completely reject. For the record, I think it does not matter where you live in the word. Your principles and your working professionalism stays with you is my personal experience, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Kinis has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Referring back to your statement, P675, and paragraph 59. Last sentence: We observed the Croatian military had set up check-points just outside the cemetery. It means Gracac cemetery. My question is, was there some other purpose for setting up these check-points or just securing area of entrance of cemetery?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told us it was for security and we were also part of the people that we were to -- were controlled in terms of that first visit. We were not allowed through because of that security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, but there was some -- some junctions with roads or some other reasons why these check-points were set up in this specific area.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The check-point was at the gate of Gracac cemetery alongside the road. It was not near a road junction. It was to control access into and out of the graveyard in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And next question is referring to paragraph 76. You mentioned regarding incident of Grubori, and there is -- you mention there was nowhere forests and it is -- based on our previous testimonies, there was some information that shared by witnesses that terrorists fled to forests and -- and ran away from this area. Can you please describe vicinity of this area and besides of it, how far was railway road from this Grubori village?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The railway road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I understand. Grubori would be, as I described, up a steep incline. There were trees around it. The middle area of the valley, if Grubori, if you imagine goes up to the right, is flat and completely clear. We could see the trees in front of Grubori from the other side of the valley where we were at the meeting. I would not say there's a large forest area in the vicinity of Grubori. There are trees or stocks of trees but not a forest, which I think, for me is a distinctly different thing. The railway line from Plavno valley would be the railway line running out from Knin up to Strmica and onwards. I would put it maybe 20 kilometres away from the area of Plavno valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately. I can't be dead sure but it was certainly some distance. You wouldn't drive out five minutes and find the railway line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: And last question is referring paragraph 81, regarding Grubori incident as well, you mentioned that we counted about 12 that houses that had been burned and been on fire and burned. My question is was these houses close to each other or they were scattered? How could you explain this situation? Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Houses were very close to each other. They were very small dwellings, I would describe them, close. When we say streets here, very, very narrow to talk down. You couldn't drive cars down any part of Grubori and the houses were quite close together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: But what was your impression, was all houses set on fire intentionally or there was some houses which are incidentally burned down and maybe some other houses would continue to burn afterwards.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of that is speculation, but our view of the people there, including myself obviously, was that they were deliberately set on fire and I think in the report I submitted 29th August, I say about half of the dwellings in Grubori were on fire and burning on the first visit that morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One follow-up question on that half. Were these all adjacent dwellings or was it one on fire, one not on fire, one on fire, one -- could you further explain what you meant by half.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not maybe seven dwellings all in a row. It was scattered, maybe three small streets different parts of Grubori village were on fire, not all consistent in one area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. This then concludes your evidence, Mr. Roberts. At the beginning you said that you wanted perhaps to add something if there is anything that you're not able to say any earlier, I'm not expecting long speeches, but if there's some vital issue you would say, I wanted to say that at that moment and I didn't get the opportunity, so ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, just to say in regard to the cross-examination by the advocate for General Cermak in the first morning, there was discussion about the first meeting with General Cermak, the 7th of August or the 8th and I was shown a UN summary of the meeting. It was suggested, I think is the right word, is what I said in my report of the focus of that meeting was not what is reflected in that meeting. I, from memory, would like the Chamber to look at the 8th of August sitrep of the Sector South commander, item B, top page, which begins, from memory: I had another meeting today with General Cermak and says the issues discussed principally were freedom of movement, security, et cetera. That's for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would like to draw our attention to that document. Is that a document which in evidence? Yes, it is. I think I've -- I've heard those lines, not through memory, but by reading them. Thank you for that. Anything else, Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And just also to submit, if I can, this file was given me on the issue, I think or -- forgive me if I can't say this word --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I think it was presented in terms of my being seen as extremely biased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you don't have to worry about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not, but I would like just to say that I was invited to say whether there's anything in here that I have said in terms of giving one comment of a critical kind of human rights violations in Sector South. Right. I have gone through every single article here. I did not, in any of these articles presented me in this file, say ever that there was a critical issue on human rights. I have gone through this file and looked at every single article before the 4th of August, 1995, and after them. And I have tabled here a memorandum of my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's perhaps by mistake this you told us earlier and then the parties would look at it and I did not take any action any further on that. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We briefly discussed it. I think my colleague has a copy, I don't have one. But we can make a bar table submission which explains the witness's comments about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. at the same time the witness asked whether he could add anything orally to what he put on paper. I leave it to the parties whether they want to tender the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My position is essentially I agree with what Mr. Roberts has just said. My question was focussed on whether there was any such comment concerning human rights before the 4th of August. He has confirmed that there is no such comment. However, he wants to and he was presented a breakdown of what topics he was discussing at that time. If the Prosecution and Mr. Roberts wish to tender that, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say it is not a direct answer to your question, the answer has been given by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He has given it orally now, but if there's a need for the Court or for the Prosecution to tender an analysis of what he was talking about, that is it fine, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, the only issue is your comments as published on human rights issues. That's what was the question was about, if would you like to add something to that, because I do understand that in your memo that -- it's mainly what subjects were covered and not any further comments on the human rights issues. Then have you an opportunity to do, but very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very briefly that having reviewed this in my memo which you have, besides myself there were other senior United Nations officials commented on all these issues here and as well as after the 4th of August 1995 and before and not one of them also with the opportunity of a journalist raised the issue of human rights in Sector South, Sector North also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say you were in good company.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that it was not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then you still owe me one answer to one question I asked you to consider. It is about the freedom of movement of journalists after the 4th of August, 1995. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. After the 4th of August 1995 the situation was very different from before. There were restrictions on some journalists going to sensitive places to report by mainly a mixture the Croatian police military and special police units and so on, but they were getting out more and more, especially in the company of UN personnel in UN vehicles, as you pushed the window on freedom of movement, they could see for themselves and reported freely what their observations were and I think there's good evidence to suggest a broad range view that -- of the activities and operations taking place, but yes, it was much better freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. This then concludes your testimony in this Court, Mr. Roberts. I would like to thank you very much for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and the Bench. We even got for free some advice with it, but that is not something I would specifically thank you for, although I appreciate your good intentions. We wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We stand adjourned, and I got it from Mr. Registrar. Thank you. We stand adjourned until tomorrow, Thursday, the 24th of July, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of July, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.
